newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's Tudjman says he'll run in '97 election.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Tudjman says he'll run in '97 election.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman, reported suffering from an incurable stomach cancer, said in a television interview on Friday he planned to run in the country's next presidential election due this year.
"If you ask me if I will run for another presidential term, the answer is yes," the 74-year president told CNN television in an expressly upbeat mood.
He also said speculation about his health was exaggerated.

"My state of health is satisfactory and it is improving very well. I can perform not only my presidential duties without difficulties, but I also enjoy playing tennis," Tudjman said in hesitant, strongly accented English.

Political analysts and diplomats in Zagreb had speculated that the former World War Two partisan and communist general, who steered Croatia to independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991-95, would step down before the presidential election due in June or July.

Some foreign analysts have expressed concern for the stability of Croatia in the event of Tudjman's departure, saying there is no obvious successor within or outside his ruling party, the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ).
Tudjman was treated in a U.S. military hospital near Washington in November for what U.S. diplomats said was a terminal-stage stomach cancer.
Croatian state-controlled media, which treated the issue of his health as a secret, said simply that he had an ulcer.
But independent Croatian weeklies, citing local medical circles, said Tudjman was seriously ill and was undergoing daily infusions of blood and nutrients to stop him losing too much weight.
In early January Tudjman vanished from public life for two weeks, only to reappear in apparently better health, although much thinner than three months ago.
Asked directly by the CNN anchorman on Friday to comment on his reported diagnosis, Tudjman said:
"There was some information that exaggerates my situation."
Asked again if that meant that these reports were wrong, Tudjman said: "In some way, yes."
In recent weeks Tudjman has clearly tried to convince the Croatian public that he is well and able to perform his duties.
Tudjman is seen as a key player in the network of Balkan peace deals, including the pact in Eastern Slavonia, where local Serbs have agreed to accept Croatian rule by mid-1997.
His influence over hardline Bosnian Croats is also a crucial factor in maintaining a fragile Moslem-Croat federation, a pillar of the U.S.-brokered Dayton peace agreement.
